summary: Defines a general set of parameters that describe the characteristics of network elements and are used to control them in the IETF integrated services framework. Different services can then share the same parameter definitions.

plainLanguage.summary: It is a shared list of measurements, like speed and delay, used to describe how each piece of the network behaves.

questions: how to describe network element delay and bandwidth
what are intserv general characterization parameters
what is path mtu in integrated services
subtitle: The shared set of numbers every Integrated Services router reports about itself, and how they add up along a path.

tldr.problem: Each Integrated Services QoS control service needs to describe network elements and traffic, and defining the same measurements again for every service would be wasteful and inconsistent.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2215 defines general parameters (such as path bandwidth, minimum latency and MTU) with fixed ID numbers, local values per network element and rules for composing them along a path.
tldr.outcome: Services such as Guaranteed and Controlled-Load share one definition of these parameters, and endpoints learn what the whole path can offer.

today: RFC 2215 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It remains the definition of these general parameters.

sections.title: General Control and Characterization Parameters
sections.content:
RFC 2215 defines the parameters used by network elements in the IETF integrated services framework. General means the parameter has the same definition and meaning across all QoS control services.

There are two kinds. Control parameters carry information from applications to the network, such as the traffic specification (TSpec). Characterization parameters describe the QoS environment along a path, for example which services are available and the estimated path bandwidth. Individual service specifications can refer to these definitions and add parameters of their own.
sections.plainLanguage: Some numbers say what you plan to send, and some say what the road can handle. This document lists the ones that are the same for everybody.

sections.title: Parameter IDs and Composition
sections.content:
Each parameter ID has two numbers: a service_number and a parameter_number, written <service_number, parameter_number>. General parameters use parameter numbers 1 to 127; numbers 128 to 254 name parameters specific to one service. Service number 1 is reserved for default values, and Guaranteed service has number 2 and Controlled-load service has number 5. The ID can form the tail of a MIB object ID, which eases network management.

Each path-characterizing parameter has a local value, which describes one network element, and composed values, which combine the incoming value with the local one by a composition rule. Composition can run downstream or upstream. Local and composed values have separate IDs so a management entity can inspect either. All definitions are conceptually per next hop, not per interface.

Every parameter has a minimal wire-representation requirement and an XDR description (RFC 1832). All parameters are mandatory for an element claiming integrated services support. For some, an element may report a reserved "indeterminate" value instead of an accurate one.
sections.plainLanguage: Each measurement has a code number, like a locker number. Each stop reports its own number and also passes along a running total or best-so-far for the trip.

sections.title: Default and Service-Specific Values
sections.content:
Often one value is right for all services at a node, so the node can export one default (global) value under service number 1. If a service needs a different value, it exports a service-specific (override) value under its own service number. The text's example: a router could report a default PATH_MTU of 1500 and a value of 250 for Guaranteed service because of scheduler or hardware limits.

The composition summary has six steps. A service-specific arriving value is composed with the local service-specific value if one exists, and otherwise with the local global value. A global arriving value is composed with the global local value, and additionally with each service-specific local value, producing new service-specific values for the next hop. Parameters numbered above 128 belong to a single service, so no global value is considered.
sections.plainLanguage: There is a normal answer for everyone. If one service needs a different answer, it gets its own, and that one wins for that service.

sections.title: The Characterization Parameters
sections.content:
NON_IS_HOP (local 1, composed 2) is a flag that is 1 when an element does not implement the relevant service. It composes with OR, so a 1 at the endpoint means some element on the path lacks support. The global flag is <1,2> and the Guaranteed-specific flag is <2,2>. If it is set, other parameters should be treated as possibly inaccurate.

NUMBER_OF_IS_HOPS (local 3, composed 4) counts integrated-services aware elements by incrementing at each one. Composed values range from 1 to 255.

AVAILABLE_PATH_BANDWIDTH (local 5, composed 6) is an estimate in bytes per second, composed with MIN. It must range from 1 byte per second to 40 terabytes per second, floating point accurate to 0.1% is encouraged, and a local value of zero means unknown.

MINIMUM_PATH_LATENCY (local 7, composed 8) is the smallest possible delay added by an element, excluding queuing. It is in microseconds, composes by summation clamped at (2**32 - 1), and that top value means indeterminate. Elements must estimate to the nearest 100 microseconds. Together with a queuing bound it lets the receiver size its de-jitter buffer.

PATH_MTU (local 9, composed 10) is the IP MTU in bytes without fragmentation, composed with MIN. A service may override with a smaller value but never a larger one.
sections.plainLanguage: The stops report whether they speak this language, how many do, how fast the slowest road is, the shortest time through, and the biggest box that fits through.

sections.title: TOKEN_BUCKET_TSPEC
sections.content:
TOKEN_BUCKET_TSPEC has parameter number 127. It is not a characterization parameter, since intermediate nodes do not export local values for it; it is a data structure shared by several services. Senders use it to describe the traffic they expect to generate.

It holds a token rate r (bytes of IP datagrams per second), a bucket depth b (bytes, from 1 byte to 250 gigabytes), a peak rate p (which may be positive infinity for unknown), a minimum policed unit m and a maximum packet size M. Datagrams smaller than m are treated as size m for allocation and policing, and m must be at most M. Larger packets may not receive QoS-controlled service. The XDR form is a struct of three floats and two unsigned integers.
sections.plainLanguage: A sender says how fast it will usually send, how big a burst it might make, how fast at top speed, and the smallest and largest packet sizes.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC says implementing these parameters creates no known new avenues for malicious attack on network infrastructure. It does reveal some additional information about a network's performance, which in extremely rare circumstances could be viewed as a security matter by the network provider.
sections.plainLanguage: Telling others how fast your roads are shares a little information, which is almost never a problem.
